data.name: Courgette Tamagoyaki
data.description: Tender golden egg layers wrap around fine green strands of courgette in this gently sweet, savoury Japanese rolled omelette. Thick breakfast slices reveal a delicate spiral and a moist, springy centre.

not_suitable_for: People with wheat allergy or coeliac disease because the soy sauce contains wheat

refrigerator.notes: Refrigerate leftovers promptly in a shallow, covered container at 4°C (40°F) or below, within 2 hours of cooking.

freezer.notes: Freeze cooled portions in an airtight container. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator; the courgette may release moisture and soften the layers.

storage.reheating: Microwave refrigerated slices in a covered, microwave-safe dish in short bursts until their centres reach 74°C (165°F). Check with a food thermometer.

equipment.name: Small nonstick tamagoyaki pan, approximately 13 × 18 cm
equipment.alternative: A 20 cm nonstick frying pan; fold the curved sides inward when rolling.

items.name: courgette
items.notes: Edible weight after trimming, before shredding and squeezing.

items.name: eggs
items.notes: Approximately 4 large eggs; weigh the contents without shells.

items.name: sunflower oil
items.notes: Divide into four 2 g portions for brushing the pan before each egg layer.

instructions.text: Finely shred the trimmed courgette using the fine grater. Keep the strands short so they will fit within thin egg layers.
Squeeze the shredded courgette firmly inside the clean kitchen cloth until no more liquid drips out readily. Discard the expressed liquid.

doneness_cues.tactile: The shreds feel damp but do not drip when compressed.

instructions.text: Beat the eggs, soy sauce and sugar in the mixing bowl with the fork until the whites are broken up and the sugar dissolves. Avoid whipping in foam.
Fold the squeezed courgette into the eggs, separating any clumps.
Preheat the pan over medium-low heat for approximately 2 minutes.
tips: The egg should sizzle gently when added, without immediately browning.

instructions.text: Fry the first layer: brush the pan with 2 g oil and spread one-quarter of the egg mixture across the base. Cook for approximately 2 minutes, until the underside holds together and the surface is moist but no longer flows.

doneness_cues.visual: The layer is pale yellow, with no pool of liquid egg.

instructions.text: Roll the first layer from the far edge towards you using the spatula, making successive folds about 3 cm wide. Position the roll at the far edge of the pan.

Fry the second layer using another 2 g oil and one-third of the remaining egg mixture. Lift the existing roll slightly so fresh egg runs beneath it. Cook for approximately 2 minutes, until the new layer holds together.
Roll the existing omelette towards you over the second layer, enclosing it snugly. Position the enlarged roll at the far edge.
Fry the third layer using another 2 g oil and half the remaining egg mixture. Let some egg run beneath the roll, then cook for approximately 2 minutes, until the layer holds together.
Roll the omelette towards you over the third layer. Position it at the far edge again.
Fry the final layer using the remaining 2 g oil and all the remaining egg mixture. Let some egg run beneath the roll, then cook for approximately 2 minutes, until the layer holds together.
Roll the omelette towards you over the final layer, finishing with the seam underneath.

Cook the completed roll over low heat for approximately 3 minutes, turning gently to warm its broad sides evenly. Check the centre from one end with the food thermometer; continue cooking until it reaches at least 71°C (160°F) before removing it from the pan.

doneness_cues.visual: The egg is fully set with no liquid escaping.
doneness_cues.tactile: The roll feels gently springy and holds its shape.

instructions.text: Rest the cooked omelette on the chopping board for 3 minutes so the layers settle before slicing.
Slice the omelette crosswise into six equal pieces with the sharp knife. Serve three slices per person on the serving plate.

troubleshooting.symptom: The layers tear or slide apart during rolling.
troubleshooting.likely_cause: The courgette contains excess moisture, the shreds are too long, or the egg layer has not set enough.
troubleshooting.prevention: Shred finely, squeeze thoroughly and let each layer become stable before rolling.
troubleshooting.fix: Fold the torn section into the centre with the spatula and enclose it in the next layer. Cook the completed roll to at least 71°C (160°F).

troubleshooting.symptom: The outside browns before the centre is cooked.
troubleshooting.likely_cause: The heat is too high for the thickening roll.
troubleshooting.prevention: Use medium-low heat for the layers and low heat for the final cooking.
troubleshooting.fix: Reduce the heat and turn the roll regularly until the centre reaches 71°C (160°F).

chef_notes: Squeezing the courgette prevents released vegetable water from separating the egg layers.
Redistribute the courgette with the fork before each pour so every layer contains a similar amount.
A slightly untidy first fold is harmless: the following layers form the outer shape.

The final centre temperature must reach 71°C (160°F); reheated leftovers must reach 74°C (165°F). [FoodSafety.gov temperature guidance](https://www.foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/safe-minimum-internal-temperatures).
data.cultural_context: Tamagoyaki is a Japanese omelette made by repeatedly rolling thin layers of seasoned egg, commonly served at breakfast and in bento. [Tamagoyaki background](https://www.justonecookbook.com/tamagoyaki/). Finely shredded courgette gives this variation green flecks and vegetable sweetness while preserving the layered preparation.
